title: Trust, and tie your camel
hookLine: the animals tell the lion to trust God, and the lion answers that effort is also God's way (Masnavi 1.900ff)
last: AM I HERE FOR THE TIME I'VE GOT.

lines: MEANT TO BE, OR ALL ON ME?
A LION IN A GREEN VALLEY.
cards: Two people wait for the same job interview. One says whatever happens is meant to be, and doesn't prepare. The other rehearses for three nights, can't sleep, and is sure it all depends on them.
Plenty of people swing between the two. Rumi's next story begins in a green valley, where the animals live in fear of a lion who hunts them whenever he likes. They go to him with an offer.
And before the story can even start, the lion and the animals get into a long argument about exactly this. Today's word is tawakkul.

teach.b: Tawakkul is an Arabic word for trust in God, relying on God, and in this story it starts an argument. The animals say to the lion: stop hunting us, and every day we'll send you one of us for your meal.
The lion is suspicious. I've been cheated before, he says; I'll hunt, I'll do my part. The animals answer with tawakkul.
Your effort is nothing, they say. Worry and scheming just show weak faith. Trust God, who feeds every creature.
The lion answers back with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
In the hadith collection of al-Tirmidhi, a man asks whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God, or tie it and trust God. The Prophet says: tie it, and trust. The lion builds on it.
God gave us hands, he says; a ladder is set in front of us, and we're meant to climb it step by step.

teach.h: THE LION: TIE IT, AND TRUST.
teach.b: Effort isn't the opposite of trust; it's one of the ways trust is lived. The argument goes back and forth for many lines, and in the end the deal is struck. What Rumi leaves you with is both halves held together.

teach.h: EFFORT IS HOW TRUST IS LIVED.
teach.b: The Quran says it in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah." Decide, act, then let go of the part that isn't yours. Before the interview: prepare, then sleep.

how: The saying 'tie your camel, and trust in God' is recorded in al-Tirmidhi's hadith collection, and in the Masnavi the lion quotes it in a long debate about tawakkul, reliance on God, and effort.

o: a hadith collection on everyday manners
accepting fate, so effort doesn't matter
trust in God, alongside doing your part

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: trust in God, relying on God

s: in the story, trust means doing nothing
the lion argues that effort is one of the ways trust is lived: tie the camel, and trust.
the tie-your-camel saying is recorded in a hadith collection
al-Tirmidhi records the Prophet telling a man: tie it, and trust.
the lion trusts the animals at once
he's suspicious, says he's been cheated before, and argues at length before the deal.

games.q: a man asks the Prophet: should I leave my camel untied and trust God, or tie it and trust God? what's the answer?
o: leave it untied; trust is enough.
tie it, and don't worry about trust.
games.why: in al-Tirmidhi's collection, the Prophet says: tie it, and trust. the lion uses this against the animals' argument.

practice: Think of one thing you're worried about and ask: what's my part? The call, the preparation, the conversation, the rope around the camel's knee; decide on it clearly.
Then ask what isn't your part, other people's choices, the weather, the outcome, and if you pray, hand that part over to God; if you don't, just open your hands and let it rest.

wordCard.voice: Tawakkul. Trust in God, relying on God, which in Rumi's story and in the Prophet's saying goes hand in hand with effort. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, also Persian: trust in God, reliance on God.

carryVoice: Your line: tie your camel. The rope and the trust go together. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah.

sources.ref: Masnavi 1.900ff (the lion and the beasts debate trust and effort)
